title: Corin and the Marsh Mystery
markdown:
Waking before dawn was damp, and so quiet Corin could hear his heart thumping a frantic drum against his ribs. That morning it was a runaway carriage. First, the barrels. Every Tuesday a dozen of the finest oak decided they had had enough and drifted into the Whispering Marsh. His job: count them. All of them. Second, the marsh itself—all that water, all that unknown depth that swallowed sunlight whole. He was the cooper’s apprentice, and he was not fond of heights, or deep water, or being too far from solid ground.

“Just count them, Corin,” Master Elms had grumbled. “Don’t let one slip your eye.” His conscience, though, was busy dreaming of a warm dry bed. Beside him sat Mist, a marsh owl with eyes like twin lamps, blinking a slow steady rhythm.

Then they appeared, bobbing like sleepy seals. One. Two. Three. Four. Five. Six. The air tasted of damp earth. Seven. Eight. Nine. His gaze flickered to the dark treeline, then back to the water. Mist let out a low resonant hoot that prickled the hairs on his neck. Barrel ten was drifting too close to a snarled willow, gnarled roots snaking from the bank. It was snagging.

“Whoa there.” His boots sank into sucking mud as he edged closer. Mist swooped and landed on the snagged barrel, talons gripping damp wood. She tilted her head, bright yellow eyes fixed on the impossibly tall reeds behind it. Barrels do not snag. They float.

Curiosity began to nudge fear aside. He pushed aside dripping branches. There, half-hidden, was a dark opening. Water flowed into it and disappeared. It smelled damp, but also dusty, with a faint intriguing metallic tang. Mist hooted again and nudged the barrel further in. It scraped stone, then settled with a soft definitive splash. An idea, born of instinct and a healthy fear of Master Elms’s scolding: they would retrieve it. The right thing.

“Right, Mist. Let’s see what’s in here.” The entrance was narrow, barely wide enough to squeeze through. The water inside was still, mirroring the gloom. His heart hammered. The walls felt slick and cold, slimy moss clinging to his fingertips. He pictured slipping, tumbling into that dark silent water, and set each boot with care.

Mist flew ahead, a silent guide. Then he saw it. Not barrels. Sacks. Piles of them, stacked high. Grain. Good honest grain, the stuff that fed the village. It was not meant to be here. Some were torn, spilling precious contents on the damp floor. Someone was hoarding the town’s food. His hands clenched. This was not just a missing barrel. This was wrong. A flicker of anger, hot and sharp, cut through the icy grip of fear. Grain for hungry bellies, not for shadowy figures to pilfer.

A harsh scraping from the entrance. Footsteps. Heavy, rough. He froze. Mist landed on his shoulder, a warm weight of silent reassurance. “Well, what have we here?” a gruff voice sneered. Two figures, silhouetted against faint daylight. Faces hard. “Looks like someone’s been snooping,” the second growled, gaze landing on him. “And an owl, too. Can’t have that.” The tunnel felt smaller. The exit impossibly far. His breath hitched.

Fear was a cold knot, but the injustice burned hotter. He remembered his grandfather: a good cooper understands the wood; it tells you what it can do. He looked at the tunnel walls—damp ancient timber. Wood. And barrels. He was an apprentice. He knew wood.

Then he saw it: a section that looked different, a plank ajar like a poorly fitted stave. Master Elms had said the right tool, used the right way, could solve almost anything. He fumbled in his apron for the small oddly shaped wedge he used for tightening hoops. A silent nod to Mist. He chipped gently at the plank’s edge.

He wedged the tool into the crack and gave it a sharp tap. Nothing. He tapped harder. A loud crack split the air, startling the smugglers. “What was that?” one shouted. “Just the tunnel settling,” the other grumbled, wary. His chance. He pushed harder. The plank groaned. A smaller opening revealed itself behind the displaced wood. Mist took flight, a silent signal. With a surge he scrambled through, rough wood tearing at his apron. Mist soared ahead, a beacon. Corin, the boy who feared water, was out in the marsh, breathing air that felt clean and exhilarating. She led him straight to the riverbank where the town guard was making their rounds.

The smugglers, caught red-handed, were apprehended swiftly. The grain was recovered. Whispers of gratitude followed him back to the cooper’s shop, louder than thunder. The marsh that morning had felt like a monstrous unknowable entity. He had walked through its belly, faced thieves, and made things right.

The barrels still floated on Tuesday mornings, a predictable rhythm in the damp air. As he counted them they did not seem so daunting. They were just barrels. And he was Corin: the cooper’s apprentice who knew how to listen to wood, and, just maybe, to himself. Fear was still a tiny whisper. A louder voice, full of quiet courage, spoke over it. He felt sturdy. Absolutely sturdy.
